key_insight: State-of-the-art visual language models reliably perform high-level object recognition but show widespread failures on standardized neuropsychological tests probing low- and mid-level visual abilities.
problem_solved: Determines whether VLMs possess the same spectrum of visual skills as humans by systematically benchmarking them on established neuropsychological tests.
method: Assembled a battery of standardized neuropsychological visual tests covering low-, mid-, and high-level functions and adapted stimuli/responses for VLM evaluation.
Ran multiple state-of-the-art VLMs on the test battery and compared model scores to human normative data and task-level breakdowns.
Analyzed per-task performance to identify systematic deficits and dissociations between high-level recognition and lower-level visual processing.
impact: Reveals a critical gap: VLMs cannot be assumed to have human-like low/mid-level vision, which affects model robustness, interpretability, and real-world deployment. Encourages development of targeted benchmarks and training objectives to close these gaps.
visual_elements: Stacked bar chart comparing VLM vs human performance across low-, mid-, and high-level test groups
Example stimulus panel showing representative tasks (e.g., texture/contour discrimination, spatial relations, object naming) with model vs human outcomes
Radar/profile plot highlighting per-test strengths and deficits for each evaluated VLM
Iconic diagram contrasting ‘high-level success’ (object icons) with ‘low/mid-level failures’ (contour, texture, spatial icons) to summarize the dissociation
paper_title: Visual language models show widespread visual deficits on neuropsychological tests
